nameStory: The 'scarlet creeper' name comes from its brilliant red flowers and vigorous climbing habit that creeps up fences, trellises, and other plants. Like other morning glories, its trumpet-shaped blooms often open in the early morning hours, though the 'scarlet' part of the name makes it clear this isn't your typical blue or purple morning glory.
description: Scarlet creeper is an annual climbing vine that produces stunning bright red, trumpet-shaped flowers. This herbaceous vine can scramble several feet up supports or trail along the ground, using its twining stems to climb. It's part of the large morning glory family and shares their characteristic funnel-shaped blooms, but stands out with its vivid scarlet color. As an annual, the entire plant grows from seed, flowers, sets seed, and dies all within one growing season.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant scarlet-red trumpet-shaped flowers about 1-2 inches across that flare out into five pointed lobes, creating an almost star-like appearance when fully open

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves that are often deeply lobed with three main sections, feeling smooth to slightly fuzzy when you run your fingers across them

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Twining vine that spirals counterclockwise around supports, with stems that feel smooth and somewhat succulent when gently squeezed

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round seed capsules that split open when mature to reveal dark, angular seeds about the size of small peppercorns

habitat: Scarlet creeper is extremely rare in New England, with only one documented observation in the region. When it does appear, it's typically in disturbed soils, garden edges, or areas with rich, well-drained soil in full sun. It prefers warm locations and may occasionally escape from cultivation or appear as a garden volunteer.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms up, and young vines begin their climbing growth with the first heart-shaped leaves appearing.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with scarlet flowers opening in early morning, often followed by afternoon closure in hot weather. Vines reach full size and continue producing flowers.
seasonality.fall: Flowers may continue into early fall in warm weather, followed by seed capsule formation. Plants begin to decline with first frost.
seasonality.winter: Annual vines are killed by frost, leaving only seeds to potentially germinate the following year.

funFact: Despite being called 'morning glory,' scarlet creeper flowers often stay open longer during the day than their blue and purple cousins, sometimes remaining open well into the afternoon to attract different pollinators like hummingbirds who are drawn to the bright red color.
confusionNotes: The bright red flowers make scarlet creeper fairly distinctive among morning glories, but it could be confused with red morning glory (Ipomoea coccinea), which has similar colored flowers but typically has more consistently heart-shaped, unlobed leaves. Remember: scarlet creeper has star-shaped flowers and often deeply lobed leaves.
contextualKnowledge: There's some naming confusion with this species - it's sometimes called 'ivy-leaved morning glory,' but that name more commonly refers to Ipomoea hederacea, a different species with purple or blue flowers. The scientific name 'hederifolia' means 'ivy-leaved,' referring to the lobed leaf shape that resembles English ivy.
compareHints: Among New England morning glories, scarlet creeper is the only one with consistently bright red flowers - common morning glory has purple flowers, ivy-leaved morning glory has blue to purple blooms, and moonflower has large white flowers. The deeply lobed, almost ivy-like leaves also help distinguish it from the more consistently heart-shaped leaves of most other morning glory species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common morning-glory has the largest flowers among New England's morning-glories, with those distinctive heart-shaped leaves that lack the three-lobed structure of ivy-leaved morning-glory.

Among New England morning-glories, ivy-leaved is distinguished by its three-lobed leaves - common morning-glory has unlobed heart-shaped leaves, while white morning-glory has much smaller flowers and often heart-shaped but sometimes three-lobed leaves.

Garden Morning Glory stands out from its Ipomoea cousins with its large flower size and vibrant blue color range - Common Morning Glory has smaller, more purple-pink flowers, while Ivy-leaved Morning Glory has distinctly lobed leaves rather than the simple heart shape.
Cypress vine is instantly distinguished from all other morning glories by its incredibly fine, thread-like leaf segments - every other morning glory in New England has broad, solid leaves.

Among its morning glory relatives, moonflower stands out for its exclusively nighttime blooming and pure white color - most other Ipomoea species bloom during the day in shades of purple, blue, pink, or red.
Unlike its morning glory relatives that are primarily grown for their showy trumpet flowers, sweet potato is grown for foliage and edible tubers, rarely flowering in New England's climate.
Red morning glory stands out from other New England morning glories primarily by its small size and brilliant red color - most others have much larger purple, blue, or white flowers.
Among New England morning-glories, wild potato vine stands out with its pure white flowers that have pink throats, while most others have purple, blue, or pink flowers.

White morning-glory stands out from its Ipomoea relatives by having the smallest flowers in the genus - much tinier than the dinner-plate-sized blooms of moonflower or the vibrant purple trumpets of common morning-glory.
